clinicalPearls: A clonal mast cell disorder with infiltration of the bone marrow and often other organs beyond the skin
Symptoms arise from mast cell mediator release (flushing, pruritus, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, anaphylaxis) and from organ infiltration
The great majority carry an activating KIT D816V mutation
A raised baseline serum tryptase supports the diagnosis and is one of the diagnostic criteria
Subtypes range from indolent systemic mastocytosis to aggressive disease and mast cell leukaemia, with markedly different prognoses
Management combines mediator-targeted symptom control and anaphylaxis preparedness with cytoreductive or KIT-targeted therapy in advanced disease
reference.pathophysiology: Systemic mastocytosis is driven by clonal proliferation of abnormal mast cells, in most cases due to an activating mutation of the KIT receptor tyrosine kinase (classically D816V), which promotes mast cell survival and accumulation. These mast cells infiltrate the bone marrow and frequently the gastrointestinal tract, liver, spleen and bone, and release mediators such as histamine and tryptase either spontaneously or in response to triggers. Symptoms therefore reflect both episodic mediator release and, in advanced forms, organ dysfunction from mast cell infiltration.
additionalInvestigations: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with mast cell immunophenotyping
Assessment for organ involvement (blood counts, liver and spleen, bone imaging)
Allergy and anaphylaxis evaluation including trigger identification
redFlags: Recurrent anaphylaxis or severe mediator crises
Cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly or malabsorption suggesting aggressive disease
reference.prognosis: Indolent systemic mastocytosis has a near-normal life expectancy with good symptom control, whereas aggressive systemic mastocytosis and mast cell leukaemia carry a poor prognosis.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent anaphylaxis to idiopathic causes without checking tryptase
Failing to provide anaphylaxis rescue medication and a trigger-avoidance plan
